questions.q: Why is summarizing a document you provide a "sweet spot" for AI?
options: AI can't make mistakes when it reads a document you paste in
AI remembers every document it was trained on, word for word
Documents are always short enough for AI to read in one go
AI is most reliable when it works from text right in front of it
questions.explain: AI is most reliable when it works from text you provide, and least reliable when it relies on memory. That doesn't make it perfect, but asking it to show its work makes it far more trustworthy.

questions.q: You want a summary of a long policy document that you can check quickly. What should you add to your prompt?
options: A request to keep the whole summary to one short paragraph
A request for a short direct quote supporting each key point
A request to fill any gaps with its best guess, so nothing is missing
A request to say how confident it feels about the summary overall
questions.explain: Supporting quotes let you check any point in seconds by searching for them in the original. Asking it to say "not in the document" rather than guessing stops it filling gaps.

questions.q: You ask AI a research question and it answers with three source links. What should you do before relying on the answer?
options: Trust it, since an answer that includes links is already verified
Ask the AI if it's sure, and accept the answer if it says yes
Open each link and check that it says what the AI claims
Find a news summary of the topic instead of the original source
questions.explain: Treating cited sources as verified is a common mistake. Open each source, check that it works and says what the AI claims, and prefer original sources like official sites or the original study.
